arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or health-risk motivation for a home bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyzer. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they value precise, non-invasive health monitoring and are willing to pay a premium for data that predicts disease risk.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (Test X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a premium home bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyzer, and use the results to decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or maintain the B2B focus.
arguments.target_customer: Health-conscious adults aged 25–55 who value precise health monitoring and are willing to pay a premium for data that predicts disease risk.
arguments.value_proposition: A stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyzer that provides accurate, non-invasive health insights, sold at a premium price with optional data subscription services.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget, analyze results against the decision rule, and decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or retain the B2B focus.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence from 1993 on consumer demand, willingness to pay, or whether privacy concerns outweigh health risk prediction.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average price willing to pay ≥ €150 and purchase intent ≥ 7/10 with health risk prediction cited as primary reason, we would proceed with the premium consumer proposition (supporting T1).

If the survey shows average price willing to pay ≤ €100 and purchase intent ≥ 7/10 with convenience/privacy cited as primary reason, we would explore a lower‑price, convenience‑focused proposition (supporting T2).

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users for personal health monitoring.
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group, such as partnering with retailers or targeting corporate wellness programs.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers.

T1.claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable, easy-to-use tool for personal health monitoring, and are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to track body composition for weight management, health improvement, or medical monitoring.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of body fat as a health risk (linked to heart disease, diabetes) and the convenience of a stand-on device in the home will motivate purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium price for a device that provides accurate, clinically relevant body-fat data, and sell accessories or subscription services for data interpretation.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for body-fat measurement.
There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to afford a premium home device.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits and accuracy of the device.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 150% of the price of a comparable commercial scale.
Pilot sales of a home version will exceed 50 units within 12 weeks if priced at €150-€200.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories or subscription services will be above 30%.
T1.first_claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable, easy-to-use tool for personal health monitoring, and are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a status symbol or a modern convenience that signals health awareness and technological sophistication, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that signals social status.
T2.who_benefits: Health-conscious consumers who use body-fat measurement as a status marker and as a way to demonstrate personal commitment to health.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing cultural emphasis on health and fitness as a status indicator, combined with the novelty of a stand-on device that provides instant data, will motivate purchase even at a premium price.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can position the device as a lifestyle accessory and command higher prices by emphasizing design, ease of use, and the perceived prestige of owning a cutting-edge health tool.
assumptions: Consumers associate body-fat measurement with elite health practices.
There is a segment of consumers willing to pay a premium for devices that signal status.
Marketing can effectively frame the device as a lifestyle accessory rather than just a health tool.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 120% of the price of a comparable commercial scale for a status-oriented version.
Pilot sales of a status-focused model will exceed 30 units within 12 weeks if priced at €180-€220.
Repeat purchase of accessories or subscription services will be below 20% due to the device’s primary role as a status item.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a status symbol or a modern convenience that signals health awareness and technological sophistication, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that signals social status.

arguments.claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable, easy-to-use tool for personal health monitoring, and are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
arguments.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to track body composition for weight management, health improvement, or medical monitoring.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of body fat as a health risk (linked to heart disease, diabetes) and the convenience of a stand-on device in the home will motivate purchase.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium price for a device that provides accurate, clinically relevant body-fat data, and sell accessories or subscription services for data interpretation.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for body-fat measurement.
There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to afford a premium home device.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits and accuracy of the device.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 150% of the price of a comparable commercial scale.
Pilot sales of a home version will exceed 50 units within 12 weeks if priced at €150-€200.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories or subscription services will be above 30%.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a status symbol or a modern convenience that signals health awareness and technological sophistication, and are willing to pay a premium for a device that signals social status.
arguments.who_benefits: Health-conscious consumers who use body-fat measurement as a status marker and as a way to demonstrate personal commitment to health.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing cultural emphasis on health and fitness as a status indicator, combined with the novelty of a stand-on device that provides instant data, will motivate purchase even at a premium price.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can position the device as a lifestyle accessory and command higher prices by emphasizing design, ease of use, and the perceived prestige of owning a cutting-edge health tool.
assumptions: Consumers associate body-fat measurement with elite health practices.
There is a segment of consumers willing to pay a premium for devices that signal status.
Marketing can effectively frame the device as a lifestyle accessory rather than just a health tool.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 120% of the price of a comparable commercial scale for a status-oriented version.
Pilot sales of a status-focused model will exceed 30 units within 12 weeks if priced at €180-€220.
Repeat purchase of accessories or subscription services will be below 20% due to the device’s primary role as a status item.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

X1.name: Consumer vs Professional Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, camping, boating) who receive a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon as a safety tool for remote emergencies. (B) Emergency responders/SAR teams who receive the same description plus information about global compatibility and mandatory registration. Both groups are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your team within the next 12 months?" (yes/no).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via outdoor activity forums and 100 emergency responder/SAR team members recruited via professional associations and government agencies.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 30% (15/50).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders/SAR teams will show purchase intent of at least 20% (20/100).

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation purchase intent >= 30% AND emergency responder purchase intent < 20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If emergency responder purchase intent >= 20% AND outdoor recreation purchase intent < 30%, conclude T2 is better supported. If both groups meet thresholds, both theories remain

final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, camping, boating) who need a reliable emergency distress signal in remote areas.
final.value_proposition: A portable 406 MHz distress beacon that provides automatic distress signals compatible with existing satellite systems and is regulated as a safety requirement, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €15,000 consumer vs professional purchase intent test (X1) with 200 participants (100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts, 100 emergency responder/SAR team members).
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and professional adoption. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows outdoor recreation purchase intent < 30% or emergency responder purchase intent >= 20%, the favoured theory would shift and the recommendation would change accordingly.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Professional Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, camping, boating) who receive a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon as a safety tool for remote emergencies. (B) Emergency responders/SAR teams who receive the same description plus information about global compatibility and mandatory registration. Both groups are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your team within the next 12 months?" (yes/no).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via outdoor activity forums and 100 emergency responder/SAR team members recruited via professional associations and government agencies.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders/SAR teams will show purchase intent of at least 20% (20/100).

arguments.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation purchase intent >= 30% AND emergency responder purchase intent < 20%, conclude T1 is better supported. frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool, because they prioritize safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who engage in activities where emergency rescue is necessary.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz frequency and is certified for emergency use will be perceived as a necessary addition to their kit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially license the technology to outdoor brands for co‑branding.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Consumers are willing to pay more for a distress beacon that is clearly labeled for emergency use.
Regulatory environment (FCC rules) permits consumer use of 406 MHz PLBs.

Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is described as a safety‑critical emergency tool versus a general safety accessory.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon through existing B2B channels, capture volume sales, and potentially secure long‑term contracts with government agencies.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool, because they prioritize safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who engage in activities where emergency rescue is necessary.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz frequency and is certified for emergency use will be perceived as a necessary addition to their kit.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially license the technology to outdoor brands for co‑branding.

Regulatory environment (FCC rules) permits consumer use of 406 MHz PLBs.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $200.
Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is described as a safety‑critical emergency tool versus a general safety accessory.

arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon through existing B2B channels, capture volume sales, and potentially secure long‑term contracts with government agencies.

predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz PLBs will increase in 2002 compared to prior years.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.

5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a 406 MHz distress beacon emphasizing either (a) outdoor safety-critical use (T1) or (b) SAR protocol integration (T2). They are asked about purchase intent (1-10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). The test also collects demographic data (age, gender, outdoor recreation frequency).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor forums) and 100 SAR/search-and-rescue professionals (recruited via SAR agency contacts). Randomly assign each participant to one of two message versions.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score (1-10) and average willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each message group.

arguments.name: Consumer vs SAR Message Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a 406 MHz distress beacon emphasizing either (a) outdoor safety-critical use (T1) or (b) SAR protocol integration (T2). They are asked about purchase intent (1-10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). The test also collects demographic data (age, gender, outdoor recreation frequency).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor forums) and 100 SAR/search-and-rescue professionals (recruited via SAR agency contacts). Randomly assign each participant to one of two message versions.
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score (1-10) and average willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each message group.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation Distress Beacon
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation groups (hikers, campers, climbers) and emergency responder/SAR communities (coast guards, search-and-rescue teams). Each participant views a product description of a 406 MHz distress beacon (specifying its 3-mile detection range, automatic activation, and registration requirement) and is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (Yes/No).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (50 hikers/campers, 50 climbers) and 100 SAR/emergency responder personnel (50 coast guards, 50 SAR teams). Participants are recruited via outdoor recreation forums, climbing clubs, and SAR agency networks.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale (1: Very unlikely to pay; 7: Very likely to pay).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show >60% purchase intent and a WTP average of at least €250 (premium price). SAR/emergency responders will show <40% purchase intent and a WTP average below €150.
prediction_by_theory.T2: SAR/emergency responders will show >50% purchase intent and a WTP average of at least €150 (volume price). Outdoor recreation participants will show <40% purchase intent and a WTP average below €250.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation purchase intent ≥60% AND WTP ≥€250, proceed with consumer product development. If SAR/emergency purchase intent ≥50% AND WTP ≥€150, explore B2B/B2G expansion. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or adoption by outdoor recreation users. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer product yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand and willingness to pay before committing resources. If the survey shows outdoor recreation purchase intent ≥60% and WTP ≥€250, proceed with a limited consumer launch; otherwise, focus on B2B/B2G expansion or licensing the technology to third parties.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) who need a reliable, long-range emergency communication device.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides automatic activation, 3-mile detection range, and mandatory registration, addressing the risk of remote emergencies for outdoor activities.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within 12 weeks at a cost of €18,000.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon in 2002.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent <40% or WTP <€250, we would abandon consumer development and focus on B2B/B2G expansion or licensing.

X1.method: Partner with 20 independent John Deere dealers in the Midwest to conduct a 12‑week pilot. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs. Brand Trust
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a convenience-focused proposition (multiple-task capability, affordability) or a brand-trust proposition (agricultural heritage, reliability). Participants are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30-65 who own a small garden (under 1/4 acre). Recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of 1962.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. Secondary measure: perceived convenience (1-5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to the convenience proposition will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than those exposed to the brand-trust proposition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to the brand-trust proposition will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than those exposed to the convenience proposition.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay between convenience-focused and brand-trust propositions. The test will determine whether homeowners in 1962 prioritize convenience or brand trust, allowing a data-driven decision on which proposition to pursue.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens in the United States who are considering purchasing a lawn and garden tractor in 1962.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes the tractor’s multiple-task capability, affordability, and ease of use, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 online survey test with 500 participants to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for convenience versus brand-trust propositions.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because the available evidence does not directly address homeowner preferences for convenience versus brand trust. The test is needed to resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a 10‑point difference in purchase intent between convenience and brand-trust groups, we would recommend developing the convenience‑focused proposition and expanding dealer support.
If the test shows no significant difference or a brand‑trust advantage, we would reconsider the investment and explore other options such as licensing tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers.

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores, and easy to maintain.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile tool that reduces chore time and cost; Deere gains a new consumer market segment.

X1.name: Dealer Survey Test
X1.method: Online survey of 500 homeowners in the United States who own small gardens (under 1/4 acre). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a standard lawn and garden tractor (price $1,200, sold through existing dealer network) and Group B receives a description of a premium lawn and garden tractor (price $1,800, sold through existing dealer network, emphasizing brand trust and agricultural heritage). Both descriptions include
X1.sample: 500 homeowners (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑Very unlikely to 7‑Very likely). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (difference between premium and standard price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A’s purchase intent will be at least 30% higher than Group B’s, because the standard tractor meets the price and convenience needs of small‑garden households.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B’s purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than Group A’s, because homeowners will pay a premium for brand trust and agricultural heritage.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent ≥ 30% and Group B’s purchase intent ≤ 20%, then T1 is supported. If Group B’s purchase intent ≥ 20% and Group A’s purchase intent ≤ 30%, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to offer a practical, inexpensive lawn and garden tractor, addressing the rapid growth of small‑garden households.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 online survey with 500 homeowners, randomizing between standard and premium descriptions.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on homeowner demand and willingness to pay through existing dealers in 1962.

arguments.method: Online survey of 500 homeowners in the United States who own small gardens (under 1/4 acre). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a standard lawn and garden tractor (price $1,200, sold through existing dealer network) and Group B receives a description of a premium lawn and garden tractor (price $1,800, sold through existing dealer network, emphasizing brand trust and agricultural heritage). arguments.sample: 500 homeowners (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑Very unlikely to 7‑Very likely). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (difference between premium and standard price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A’s purchase intent will be at least 30% higher than Group B’s, because the standard tractor meets the price and convenience needs of small‑garden households.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B’s purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than Group A’s, because homeowners will pay a premium for brand trust and agricultural heritage.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address homeowner motivations or tractor demand. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.
arguments.new_claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and economical to maintain.

arguments.quote: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA.
arguments.does_not_show: The source is a simulated warehouse packing efficiency and does not address homeowner motivations or tractor demand, so it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct the proposed Small‑Garden Owner Purchase Intent Test (X1) to gather evidence on homeowner demand and willingness to pay before committing resources.
arguments.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) in the United States who are considering purchasing a lawn and garden tractor for tasks beyond lawn mowing.
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions the tractor as a cost‑effective, practical tool for small‑garden tasks, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network to reach individual buyers.
arguments.next_action: Run the Small‑Garden Owner Purchase Intent Test (X1) with 200 homeowners, measuring purchase intent, cost‑effectiveness rating, and time‑saving rating. Use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a differentiated proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to market growth figures and a single source on demand; it does not address homeowner motivations such as cost, practicality, or time‑saving, nor does it provide data on actual purchase rates or price points.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent ≥ 60% and cost‑effectiveness ratings ≥ 3 AND time‑saving ratings ≥ 3, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑garden owners.
If the test shows purchase intent < 60%, abandon the differentiated proposition and focus on existing dealer model or other expansion options.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Direct vs Dealer Sales Test (200 units, 12 weeks, €18,000) to measure direct vs dealer sales volume and price. If direct sales meet or exceed 30% and the direct price is at least 10% above dealer price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑scale farming. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Small‑scale farmers will purchase tractors directly from Deere because they need specialized equipment for specific tasks and trust Deere’s engineering.
T1.who_benefits: Deere benefits by selling tractors directly to farmers at premium prices, bypassing dealers and capturing higher margins.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Farmers recognize Deere’s reputation for durability and reliability, and they require tractors tailored to niche operations that dealers may not offer.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells directly to farmers at higher prices, retaining full profit margin compared to dealer commissions.
assumptions: Farmers have access to information about Deere’s engineering.
Deere can design tractors for specific small‑scale farming tasks.
Direct sales to farmers are feasible and cost‑effective for Deere.
predictions: If Deere launches a line of small‑scale tractors marketed directly to farmers, purchase rates will be higher than if sold only through dealers.
Average selling price per tractor will exceed dealer markup of 20%.
T1.first_claim: Small‑scale farmers will purchase tractors directly from Deere because they need specialized equipment for specific tasks and trust Deere’s engineering.

T2.claim: Homeowners will purchase lawn and garden tractors because they find them affordable and convenient for small‑yard tasks, and they prefer a single tool over multiple hand tools.
T2.who_benefits: Deere benefits by selling directly to homeowners at retail margins, expanding its consumer market and capturing volume sales.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners see lawn tractors as a time‑saving, cost‑effective solution for mowing, edging, and light gardening, and they value the convenience of a single machine over separate hand tools.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors directly to homeowners at retail prices, earning margins comparable to dealer commissions but with higher volume.
assumptions: Homeowners have access to information about lawn tractor capabilities.
Price sensitivity drives purchase decisions for homeowners.
Deere can market tractors as a single‑tool solution for small yards.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer‑focused lawn tractor line marketed directly to homeowners, unit sales will exceed dealer‑only sales.
Average retail price will be similar to competitor offerings, but volume will be higher due to broader appeal.
T2.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase lawn and garden tractors because they find them affordable and convenient for small‑yard tasks, and they prefer a single tool over multiple hand tools.
